paper.title: Parallel random numbers: as easy as 1, 2, 3
paper.venue: SC'11 (International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis)

program.how: written for ounce-core from the algorithm in the paper; no third-party code copied
program.target: static freestanding aarch64 Linux ELF, run with `ounce-core run-elf`
program.also: smoke.c: statistical smoke tests of the generator (frequency, runs, chi-square, serial correlation, cross-stream correlation, strict avalanche), written from textbook definitions

claims_checked: Philox4x32 with 10 rounds maps counter (0,0,0,0), key (0,0) to 6627e8d5 e169c58d bc57ac4c 9b00dbd8
Philox4x32 with 10 rounds maps counter and key all ffffffff to 408f276d 41c83b0e a20bc7c6 6d5451fd
Philox4x32 with 10 rounds maps counter 243f6a88 85a308d3 13198a2e 03707344, key a4093822 299f31d0 (digits of pi) to d16cfe09 94fdcceb 5001e420 24126ea1

Statistical smoke tests (NOT the paper's BigCrush claim): on two streams of 2^20 words each (key (0,0) with sequential counters, and a second key), the frequency, runs, byte and 16-bit chi-square and lag-1 serial correlation z-scores are all within 4 sigma; two streams with keys differing in one bit are uncorrelated within 4 sigma; flipping any of 128 counter bits or 64 key bits flips each output bit with probability 1/2 within 5 sigma over 1024 random inputs (worst z 3.88). Thresholds were fixed before the first run.

expected_values_source.what: the authors' published known-answer vectors, lines beginning `philox4x32 10` in tests/kat_vectors of the Random123 distribution
expected_values_source.note: the vectors are data, copied as numbers; the file's code and text were not copied

not_checked: the paper's statistical quality claim as such (Crush and BigCrush from TestU01, which is GPL and not vendored here); the smoke tests above are far weaker and only catch gross defects
throughput and speed figures (run time under emulation says nothing about the authors' hardware)
Philox2x32, Philox2x64, Philox4x64 and the Threefry and ARS generators
published known-answer vectors for reduced-round variants (none in the file used)
Tier-4 and native ARM64 execution (the native comparison here is x86-64)
what_a_pass_means: this program, run on ounce-core, produces exactly the published outputs for these three inputs, and the generator passes a battery of simple statistical tests that a 6-round version fails. It does not show the paper's wider claims (BigCrush, speed) are correct.
observations: Negative control for the smoke tests: the same tests applied to Philox with fewer rounds fail for 1 to 6 rounds (13, 13, 12, 5, 3 and 2 failing statistics) and pass at 7 rounds and above, so the battery can tell a weak generator from a strong one; this is an observation about this battery, not a statement about the paper's round-count analysis
Output of both programs on ounce-core Tier-3 is identical to a native x86-64 build
